Non-Additive Effects of Mental, Physical, and Sleep Fatigue on Human Postural Control

Jeevan Jayasuriya, Heather D. Bean, Roozbeh Jafari, Steven E. Riechman, Ranjana K. Mehta
NeuroErgonomics Lab · University of Wisconsin–Madison

Introduction

Human postural control as a feedback system

1
Sense

Integrating visual, vestibular, and somatosensory information.1

2

3

CoP ellipse area quantifies the spatial extent of postural sway.2

Introduction

In practice, fatigue types rarely occur alone

Industrial work
  • Oil rig studies: physical & mental demands,1 sleep loss2
  • Manufacturing: fatigue due to short sleep, stress and shift schedules3
  • Construction: higher accident risk under lack of sleep4
Emergency & space operations
  • EMS: fatigue causes twice the odds of injury5
  • Firefighting: balance impairments, more so with increased work time6
  • Apollo missions: mental fatigue on the lunar surface7
Healthcare
  • Nurses: postural sway increased by ~14% after three 12-hour shifts7
  • Medical residents: slow response to balance disturbances after on-call nights8
The gapDoes combined fatigue effects on postural control simply add up when workers face more than one at once?
[1] Kang et al., 2024; Bazazan et al., 2023 [2] Bhuanantanondh et al., 2021 [3] Lu et al., 2017 [4] Powell & Copping, 2010 [5] Barger et al., 2014 [6] Scheuring et al., 2007 [7] Thompson et al., 2016 [8] Ungar et al., 20234
Introduction

Why physical-fatigue pairings are expected to be worst

Physical fatigue↓ force capacity, proprioception2
Sleep loss↓ sensory integration, central regulation1
Mental fatigue↓ attention, cognitive control4
Postural controlattention · sensory integration · motor output5
SP Sleep + physical

Physical fatigue adds a muscular and proprioceptive deficit to sleep loss.1,2

Expected: less effective muscular compensation for sleep-related impairment

MP Mental + physical

Physical fatigue raises the attentional demands of balance.3 Mental fatigue impairs goal-directed attention.4

Expected: less attention-based compensation for physical fatigue

SM Sleep + mental

Both act mainly on sensory, central and attentional processes; neither directly reduces muscular capacity.1

Expected: a smaller increase than the physical pairings

[1] Paillard, 2023   [2] Paillard, 2012   [3] Simoneau et al., 2006   [4] Boksem & Tops, 2008   [5] Woollacott & Shumway-Cook, 20025
Introduction

Hypothesis

Balance changes will depend on the stressor and pairing, with the greatest impairment when physical fatigue combines with another fatigue state.

Methods

Within-subject, counterbalanced study

72
participants analyzed
44 males and 28 females
Age 23.1 ± 5.34 years
Weeks 1–2Screening and orientationWeeks 3–7Five weekly fatigue sessions
12
counterbalanced orders

Mental and physical sessions first, then the three combined conditions.

7
Methods

Fatigue induction protocols

Mental fatigueVisuospatial 2-back, 2 h
n − 2
n − 1
n
Same spot as two back → press
  • Match probability 25%
  • 500 ms stimulus, 1.5–2 s interval
  • 4 × 30-min blocks; engagement monitored in real time
Physical fatigueLoaded treadmill rucking, 2 h
47%of lean body mass carried in a rucksack
Steady · 15 minTime trial · 15 min
One 30-min block, repeated × 4
  • Steady state at a speed eliciting 47% VO₂peak
  • Time trial: self-paced, covering maximum distance
Sleep deprivationExtended wakefulness
28 hof continuous wakefulness
  • Wake at 06:00; no naps; no caffeine after breakfast
  • In lab from 18:00
MP: 2-back answered with a handheld clicker while rucking.   SM / SP: the 10:00 mental or physical fatigue task after the overnight session.

Methods

Experimental controls

Nutrition

Standardized meals for 30 hours before each session

Hydration and fueling

Carbohydrate–electrolyte drink (physical); water (mental)

Environment

Thermoneutral laboratory, uniform lighting

Monitoring

Continuous wearable monitoring of sleep and activity (7 weeks)

Task familiarization

To minimize learning effects

10
Methods

Balance assessment and sway outcomes

Modified Clinical Test of Sensory Interaction on Balance (mCTSIB)
Protocol

Four activities, 30 seconds each, two trials per activity

Recording

AMTI force plate at 1000 Hz, low-pass filtering at 10 Hz

OutcomeSway area: 95% CoP confidence ellipse (cm²)
11
Methods

Statistical analysis

Linear mixed-effects model, per balance task
Outcome ~ Fatigue Type × Phase + (1 | Participant)
Factors

Six fatigue types (M, P, S, MP, SM, SP) and two phases: PRE and POST

Models

Separate linear mixed-effects models (LMM) for each balance task

Fatigue Type × PhaseDoes the change from PRE to POST differ by fatigue type within each activity?

Discussion

The hypothesis was partially supported

Hypothesis: balance changes depend on fatigue type and pairing, with the greatest impairment when physical fatigue combines with another fatigue state.
✓Supported
  • Type-specific effects: Fatigue Type × Phase significant in all four activities
  • SP: significant in all four activities; highest overall percentage change from PRE to POST
✕Not supported
  • MP: not consistently among the most impaired; n.s. on foam with eyes open (+3.5%)
17
Discussion

Discussion

1
Sleep loss exacerbated physical-fatigue deficits

Rig studies measured fatigue and vigilance but not balance.1–3 Assess balance after demanding work following a night shift.

SP highest overall (95%)
2
Sleep deprivation impaired balance in every activity

Contrary to reports of preserved balance under sleep deprivation.3,4

S significant in 4 of 4 activities
3
Mental fatigue effects did not grow with task difficulty

Switch from automatic to cognitively mediated regulation under harder tasks;5,6 high baseline attentional demands.

M +25% → −6% as difficulty increased
[1] Kang et al., 2024; Bazazan et al., 2023 [3] Cheng et al., 2018 [4] Stemplewski et al., 2023 [5] Gupta & Singla, 2024 [6] Woollacott & Shumway-Cook, 200218
Discussion

Limitations

Sway area is a top-level outcome

Same sway, different underlying neurophysiological costs.1–5

Healthy young adults

Healthy adults in their early twenties (mean about 23 years). Older adults, clinical populations, or experienced industrial workers may respond differently.

Quiet standing only

Dynamic tasks such as walking, carrying loads, recovering from perturbations, or balancing while doing a secondary task were not tested.

Time of day

Sleep conditions compare evening PRE with morning POST, so time of day is a possible confound.
